title: Restorative Drugs (Vitamins and Minerals)
path: Drugs Used for Conditions Apart from Systemic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction to Restorative Drugs: Vitamins and Minerals
headings.content: Restorative drugs are therapeutic agents utilized to restore or maintain normal physiological functions by replacing essential micronutrients that the body cannot synthesize in sufficient quantities. Vitamins are organic compounds required in minute amounts for cellular metabolism, growth, and immune function. Minerals are inorganic elements that serve structural roles, maintain fluid balance, and act as cofactors for enzymatic reactions. Within the Nigerian healthcare landscape, micronutrient supplementation plays a critical role in public health initiatives, particularly in combating endemic deficiencies among vulnerable populations such as pregnant women and under-five children. These substances do not provide direct caloric energy, yet they dictate how the body processes carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. Understanding their baseline biochemical roles enables clinicians to distinguish between physiological requirements and pharmacological interventions.

headings.title: Classification and Sources of Vitamins
headings.content:
Vitamins are divided into two distinct groups based on their solubility, which dictates their absorption, transport, and storage characteristics within the body.

- **Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, and K)**: Dissolve in lipids, require bile salts for intestinal absorption, and are stored in the liver and adipose tissue. Because of body storage, excessive intake can lead to accumulation and toxicity. Rich sources include palm oil, liver, egg yolks, and green leafy vegetables.
- **Water-Soluble Vitamins (Complex B and Vitamin C)**: Dissolve in water, are readily absorbed into the bloodstream, and excess amounts are excreted via renal filtration. They require daily replenishment because minimal reserves are stored. Rich sources include citrus fruits, beans, whole grains, and lean meats.

headings.title: Classification and Sources of Minerals
headings.content:
Minerals are categorized into macro-minerals and trace elements based on the quantitative amounts required by the human body daily.

| Mineral Category | Daily Requirement | Common Examples | Primary Dietary Sources |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Macro-minerals | Greater than 100 mg | Calcium, Magnesium, Potassium | Dairy products, legumes, salt |
| Trace Minerals | Less than 100 mg | Iron, Zinc, Iodine | Red meat, shellfish, iodized salt |

Macro-minerals maintain fluid balance, bone matrix rigidity, and neuromuscular irritability. Trace minerals, though required in minute quantities, are vital constituents of enzymatic systems, oxygen transport molecules, and hormonal synthesis pathways.

headings.title: Pharmacokinetics and Mechanism of Action
headings.content:
Once ingested, vitamins and minerals undergo liberation from food matrices or pharmaceutical formulations, followed by absorption across the gastrointestinal mucosa. Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum, requiring an acidic gastric environment for optimal ionization. Calcium absorption is heavily dependent on the active metabolite of vitamin D, calcitriol. 

At the cellular level, these agents function primarily as coenzymes, structural stabilizers, or electron donors. For instance, B-complex vitamins act as coenzymes in the Krebs cycle to facilitate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production. Vitamin C acts as a powerful antioxidant, neutralizing reactive oxygen species. Distribution occurs via plasma transport proteins to target tissues, where cellular uptake is tightly regulated by homeostatic feedback loops before renal or biliary elimination.

headings.title: Clinical Indications and Therapeutic Uses
headings.content: Therapeutic supplementation of vitamins and minerals is indicated for primary prevention, treatment of established deficiency states, and management of increased physiological demands. Pregnant and lactating women require increased iron and folic acid to support expanded maternal blood volume and prevent neural tube defects in the fetus. Therapeutic doses of iron are prescribed for microcytic hypochromic anemias, while calcium and vitamin D combinations are standard prophylactic therapy against osteoporosis in postmenopausal populations. In clinical practice across tropical regions, high-dose vitamin A supplementation is routinely administered during measles campaigns to reduce mucosal morbidity and mortality. Supplementation is also crucial for patients undergoing bariatric surgery or those experiencing malabsorption syndromes.

headings.title: Nutritional Deficiencies and Associated Syndromes
headings.content: Prolonged inadequate intake, impaired absorption, or excessive metabolic loss of micronutrients leads to recognizable clinical deficiency syndromes. Vitamin A deficiency manifests initially as night blindness, progressing to xerophthalmia and permanent corneal scarring if untreated. Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency results in beriberi, characterized by peripheral neuropathy and cardiovascular failure, or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome frequently observed in chronic alcohol dependency. Iron deficiency leads to microcytic anemia, presenting with pallor, fatigue, and koilonychia. Iodine deficiency remains a major global cause of preventable mental impairment and goiter formation in non-iodized salt regions.

headings.title: Adverse Effects and Toxicity of Supplementation
headings.content: While essential for health, restorative drugs can produce adverse effects and acute or chronic toxicity when consumed in excessive quantities. Iron supplements commonly cause gastrointestinal irritation, nausea, constipation, and dark-colored stools. Acute iron poisoning, particularly in young children who ingest adult supplements, is a medical emergency causing corrosive mucosal damage and systemic shock. Chronic high-dose intake of fat-soluble vitamins, such as Vitamin A, can lead to hepatotoxicity, intracranial pressure elevation, and teratogenic effects in pregnancy. Excessive vitamin C intake may precipitate osmotic diarrhea and increase the risk of kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment, Patient Education, and Administration Guidelines
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care involves thorough nutritional assessments, baseline laboratory evaluations, and targeted patient education to ensure safe and effective therapy. Nurses must evaluate dietary habits, gastrointestinal symptoms, and medication histories to identify actual or potential deficiencies. Oral iron should be administered between meals with citrus juice to enhance absorption, though it can be given with food if gastric upset is intolerable. Liquid iron preparations require the use of a straw to prevent permanent staining of the dental enamel. Patient education must emphasize that supplements complement rather than replace a balanced diet and that keeping vitamins out of the reach of children prevents accidental pediatric toxicity.
